parole.significato: who works in a quick and accurate manner, able to do something very quickly yet still very accurately; nimble, deft
parole.testo: From Low German flink (“agile, quick”), probably from Middle Low German vlinken (“shining”). Perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *flakurōną (“to flutter, beat repeatedly”).

parole.significato: ridiculously small and insignificant, measly, paltry, petty
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German futtig, likely from Proto-Germanic *fuþiz.
From Low German günnen, from Old Saxon giunnan, from Proto-Germanic *gaunnaną. See gunst and unna.

Attested since 1529, from Low German jolle, from Middle Low German jolle, possibly ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlos (“tube”), see also Lithuanian aulas, Norwegian aul, Hittite [script needed] (auli-, “tube-shaped organ in the neck”), Albanian hollë, Latin a
From Low German manen, from Old Saxon manon, from Proto-Germanic *manōną, cognate with Old English manian (“to remind”).

parole.significato: loose, slippery, partly melted snow, often mixed with mud
parole.testo: From Low German mode, from Middle Low German modder (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“sediment”).

From Low German not, nut, from Proto-Germanic *hnōjaną (“to smooth, join together”), from Proto-Indo-European *kneh₂-. Cognate with Danish not, Norwegian Bokmål not, Norwegian Nynorsk not, nót and German Nut.

From Low German nat, naad, from Middle Low German nāt, from Old Saxon nād, from Proto-Germanic *nēdiz (“that which is sewn; seam; stitch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin (thread), to sew”). Cognate with Danish nåd, Norwegian Bokmål nat, Norwegian Nynorsk nat, German Naht and Dutch naa
From Low German shel, schele, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *skiljaną (“to divide, split”).
From Old Swedish skør, skyr, from Low German schör (“weak, fragile”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *skuriz, derived from the verb *skeraną (“to cut”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk skjør.
From Low German and Middle Low German slange, from Old Saxon slango, from Proto-Germanic *slangô.

parole.significato: to speak unclearly (due to poor articulation), to slur
parole.testo: From Low German sludern, from a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber. Compare also Dutch slodderen (“to be sloppy”).
